Neonatal calves emerge after a gestation period that averages approximately 227 days [tg = approximately 227 days], a duration that aligns closely with values reported for other small-bodied at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]forest duikers. Weaning, marking the complete cessation of lactation, occurs at 100 days after birth [tx = 100 days after birth], a relatively brief suckling period given the calf's degree of precocial development at birth at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. The maximum daily reproductive rate for this species is realized as approximately one calf per year [Ri = approximately one calf per year], a pattern consistent with the slow life-history pace typical of tropical ungulates. This restricted reproductive output, combined with the substantial maternal investment required by a single large neonate, reflects the energetic constraints imposed by its dense rainforest habitat.

Sexual maturation in the Zebra duiker exhibits a pronounced sexual dimorphism in timing. Females reach puberty at 320 days [tp = 320 days] after birth, a value that falls within the range of 9 to 12 months reported in captive studies of congeneric species at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. Males, in contrast, require a considerably longer developmental period, attaining reproductive maturity at 457 days [tp = 457 days] after birth at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C]. This delayed maturation in males is likely associated with the need to achieve a body size and social standing sufficient to compete for access to breeding territories. Both pubertal milestones were established from longitudinal records of captive individuals housed under thermal conditions approximating the species' natural tropical environment.

Considerable sexual dimorphism is evident in the adult body mass of the Zebra duiker. Females ultimately reach an asymptotic adult mass of 17.5 kilograms [Wwi = 17.5 kilograms], whereas males attain a slightly lower ceiling of 17.0 kilograms [Wwi = 17.0 kilograms]. This pattern of female-biased size dimorphism is unusual among ungulates and may be linked to the energetic demands of gestation and prolonged lactation in a species that produces a single, relatively precocial calf. Field records indicate that these asymptotic masses are reached by approximately three to four years of age, after which growth plates fuse and skeletal development ceases. The substantial adult mass, combined with a relatively modest home range, suggests an efficient foraging strategy centered on nutrient-dense forest fruits.

Neonatal mass at birth also differs between the sexes, reflecting an early-life investment asymmetry. Female calves are born with a wet body weight of 1450 grams [Wwb = 1450 grams], a value that corresponds to roughly 8.3 percent of the maternal adult mass. Male neonates share this identical birth mass of 1450 grams [Wwb = 1450 grams], despite the ultimate difference in adult body size between the sexes. Available surveys report a range extending from 1.27 to 1.55 kilograms for females and from 1.3 to 1.75 kilograms for males, indicating some variability likely driven by maternal condition and litter position. The relatively heavy birth mass, characteristic of precocial ungulates, enables the calf to follow the mother within hours of parturition, a critical anti-predator adaptation.

Longevity data for the Zebra duiker indicate a maximum lifespan of 4745 days [am = 4745 days] when measured under controlled captive conditions at 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C], which is equivalent to approximately 13 years. This lifespan is notably extended for a mammal of its body size, exceeding predictions based on mass-scaling relationships and suggesting a slow aging rate characteristic of species with low extrinsic mortality in predator-limited environments. Senescence in captive individuals typically manifests as progressive dental wear and a decline in locomotor ability after the tenth year. The combination of a long maximum lifespan, late sexual maturation in males reaching puberty at 457 days after birth [tp = 457 days after birth], and a low annual reproductive rate of one calf per year [Ri = one calf per year] firmly positions the Zebra duiker as a slow-living, K-selected species at a temperature of 39.4 °C [T = 39.4 °C].
